lessons.title: Why test? Yield, defect level and the cost of escapes

scenes.text: A phone maker returns 1,200 faulty chips from a lot of one million. The fab says every chip passed final test.
The test engineer checks the fault coverage report: only 90% of modelled faults were exercised. The escapes were always going to happen.

steps.title: Verification vs testing
steps.body:
**Verification** checks that the *design* meets its specification (done once, before tape-out). **Testing** checks that each *manufactured copy* is free of physical defects (done on every chip, at wafer sort and final test). Testing cannot find design bugs; verification cannot find dust particles.

Defects arise from particles, lithography errors, via voids, gate-oxide pinholes and contamination. **Yield** Y is the fraction of good chips; **defect level** DL is the fraction of *shipped* chips that are bad, usually quoted in DPM (defective parts per million).

steps.title: Williams-Brown model
steps.body:
With yield Y and fault coverage T (0 to 1):

**DL = 1 − Y^(1−T)**

If T = 1, DL = 0. If T = 0, DL = 1 − Y (all bad chips escape). The model shows that low-yield processes need very high coverage to reach low DPM.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Y = 0.9, T = 0.99. DL = 1 − 0.9^0.01 = 1 − 0.998946 = 0.001054 = **1054 DPM**. Raising T to 0.999 gives about 105 DPM, so each extra 9 in coverage cuts DPM by ten.

steps.title: Rule of ten
steps.body: Finding a fault costs roughly ten times more at each level: chip, board, system, field. This is why coverage targets of 98 to 99+% are common for automotive and server parts.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing yield with fault coverage.
- Using the percentage 90 instead of 0.90 in the exponent.
- Believing 100% stuck-at coverage means zero defects: other defect types (delay, bridging) may still escape.

activity.prompt: Y = 0.8 and fault coverage T = 0.95. Compute the defect level in DPM (round to nearest whole number).

quiz.why: DL = 1 − Y^(1−T); with T = 1 the exponent is 0 so Y^0 = 1 and DL = 0.

lessons.title: Fault models: stuck-at, bridging, delay, stuck-open

scenes.text: A particle shorts an internal net to VDD. Whatever the logic says, the net reads 1.
Instead of modelling every particle, the test engineer models the effect: net n1 stuck-at-1.

steps.title: Why fault models
steps.body: Physical defects are too varied to enumerate. A **fault model** is an abstraction that maps defects to logical behaviour so ATPG and fault simulation can be automated. A good model is simple, covers many real defects and is technology independent.

steps.title: Main models
steps.body:
- **Single stuck-at (SSA):** one line permanently 0 (s-a-0) or 1 (s-a-1); all others fault free. For a circuit with N lines there are **2N** faults.
- **Bridging:** two nets shorted; behaves as wired-AND, wired-OR or dominant driver.
- **Transition / gate-delay:** slow-to-rise or slow-to-fall at a node; needs two-vector tests.
- **Path-delay:** the cumulative delay of a path exceeds the clock period.
- **Stuck-open (transistor):** a broken transistor makes the output float and remember its previous value, so a **two-pattern** test is needed in CMOS.
- **IDDQ:** abnormal quiescent supply current exposes bridges and oxide shorts.

steps.title: Worked example: fault counting and collapsing
steps.body:
A 2-input NAND with inputs a, b and output z has 3 lines, so 6 single stuck-at faults.

Equivalence: a s-a-0, b s-a-0 and z s-a-1 all give z = 1 for every input, so they are indistinguishable. Keep one representative: collapsed set = a s-a-1, b s-a-1, z s-a-0 plus one of the equivalent trio = **4 faults**.

General rule: an n-input NAND/AND/OR/NOR has 2(n+1) faults, which collapse to **n+2**.

steps.title: Worked example: dominance
steps.body: For the NAND, test for z s-a-0 needs z = 1 in the good circuit, which happens for inputs 00, 01, 10. The test for a s-a-1 is (a,b)=(0,1) which also detects z s-a-0. So z s-a-0 *dominates* a s-a-1 and can be dropped from the target list: checkpoint set = **a s-a-0/1, b s-a-0/1 on primary inputs and fanout branches**.

steps.title: Checkpoint theorem
steps.body: Testing all stuck-at faults on checkpoints (primary inputs and fanout branches) detects all single stuck-at faults in a combinational circuit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a stuck-open fault is detected by one vector; it needs an initialisation vector then a test vector.
- Counting faults only on gate outputs and forgetting inputs and fanout branches.
- Collapsing equivalent faults on a XOR gate: XOR has no input equivalences.

story.title: How good is my test set?

scenes.text: The team has 500 patterns but no number to prove they are good.
A fault simulator applies each pattern to the good circuit and to faulty copies and counts the differences at outputs.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
**Fault coverage (FC)** = detected faults / total faults.
**Test coverage** = detected / (total − untestable).
**Fault efficiency (ATPG effectiveness)** = (detected + proven untestable) / total.
**Untestable (redundant)** faults cannot change any output, usually because of redundant logic.

steps.title: Simulation algorithms
steps.body:
- **Serial:** simulate one fault at a time; simple, slow.
- **Parallel:** pack W faulty machines into one machine word, bitwise operations.
- **Deductive:** propagate lists of faults that make each line differ from the good value.
- **Concurrent:** keep only the *differences* of faulty machines (event driven), the industrial workhorse.
- **Fault dropping:** once detected, a fault is removed from further simulation, speeding later patterns.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
Total faults 1000; detected 940; proven untestable 20; aborted 40.

Fault coverage = 940/1000 = **94.0%**.
Test coverage = 940/(1000−20) = **95.9%**.
ATPG effectiveness = (940+20)/1000 = **96.0%**.

steps.title: Worked example 2: parallel simulation cost
steps.body: A 32-bit machine word simulates 31 faults plus the good machine per pass. For 6200 faults one pattern needs ceil(6200/31) = **200 passes**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating redundant faults as ATPG failures: they should be removed from the denominator for test coverage.
- Believing fault dropping lowers final coverage; it only saves time.

activity.prompt: Total faults 2000, detected 1860, untestable 40. Test coverage (%) = detected/(total − untestable). Give the value to one decimal.

options: Removing detected faults from further simulation

lessons.title: Testability measures: SCOAP controllability and observability

scenes.text: A gate deep inside a block takes ATPG ten minutes to justify, while an input gate takes milliseconds.
SCOAP numbers predict this difficulty before ATPG even runs.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **CC0(l), CC1(l)**: combinational 0/1-controllability, the effort to set line l to 0 or 1. **CO(l)**: combinational observability, effort to propagate a value on l to a primary output. Primary inputs: CC0 = CC1 = 1. Primary outputs: CO = 0. Larger = harder.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- AND: CC1(z) = ΣCC1(inputs) + 1; CC0(z) = min CC0(inputs) + 1.
- OR: CC0(z) = ΣCC0(inputs) + 1; CC1(z) = min CC1(inputs) + 1.
- NOT: CC0(z) = CC1(a) + 1; CC1(z) = CC0(a) + 1.
- Observability of input a of AND: CO(a) = CO(z) + CC1(other inputs) + 1 (others must be non-controlling = 1). For OR use CC0 of others.
- Fanout stem: CO(stem) = min over branches.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Chain of three 2-input ANDs with all other inputs PIs: z1 = a·b, z2 = z1·c, z3 = z2·d. CC1: z1 = 3, z2 = 3+1+1 = 5, z3 = 5+1+1 = **7**. Long AND chains make logic-1 expensive; this motivates test points.

steps.title: Use
steps.body: Tools use SCOAP to choose easier paths in PODEM backtrace and to place **test points**: control points raise controllability, observation points raise observability.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using min instead of sum for the hard value (CC1 of AND).
- Forgetting the +1 for each gate level.
- Forgetting that sequential SCOAP has separate SC/SO measures counting flip-flop depth.

lessons.title: Lab: Minimal test sets for gates and redundancy

scenes.text: The bench has a 4-input NAND on a breadboard. Exhaustive testing needs 16 vectors.
Using fault models, the lab guide reaches full stuck-at coverage with five.

steps.title: Aim and apparatus
steps.body: Aim: derive the minimum test set detecting all single stuck-at faults of an n-input NAND gate. Apparatus: logic trainer or simulator, 74xx NAND, LEDs.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body:
Input s-a-0: the input must be 1 and all others 1 (non-controlling) so the output flips from 0 to 1: needs vector 11...1.
Input i s-a-1: input i = 0, others = 1: output good = 1, faulty = 0.
Output faults are covered by those vectors.

Vectors needed: one all-ones + n single-zero vectors = **n+1**. For a 4-input NAND: 5 vectors.

steps.title: Redundancy example
steps.body: f = a·b + a·b' reduces to a. In the unminimised circuit, the fault 'b s-a-1 on the first AND' is untestable... check: the term a·b' and a·b make f = a regardless of b, so b-related faults produce no change at f: **redundant**. Removing redundancy gives f = a and removes untestable faults.

steps.title: Observations table
steps.body: Record good output and faulty output for each vector in your lab book. A vector detects a fault if they differ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying all vectors but not recording faulty responses.
- Assuming redundant faults are tester failures.

lessons.title: Activation, propagation, justification and the Boolean difference

scenes.text: To catch a stuck-at fault the tester must first excite it, then carry its effect to an output.
A mathematician sees this as one formula: the Boolean difference.

steps.title: The three steps
steps.body:
1. **Activation:** set the fault site to the value opposite to the stuck value.
2. **Propagation:** set side inputs along a path so the fault effect appears at a primary output (sensitised path).
3. **Line justification:** find primary-input values that create all the needed internal values (consistency).

steps.title: Boolean difference
steps.body: For f(x1..xn), **∂f/∂xi = f(xi=0) ⊕ f(xi=1)**. A test for xi s-a-0 is any vector with xi = 1 and ∂f/∂xi = 1; for xi s-a-1: xi = 0 and ∂f/∂xi = 1.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: f = ab + c. ∂f/∂a = (c) ⊕ (b + c) = b·c'. So a s-a-0 is tested by a=1, b=1, c=0 (good f = 1, faulty f = 0). a s-a-1 is tested by a=0, b=1, c=0 (good 0, faulty 1).

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: f = (a+b)·c. ∂f/∂c = (a+b)⊕0 = a+b. Tests for c s-a-0: c=1 and a+b = 1, e.g. 101. Number of vectors that test c s-a-0 = 3 (101, 011, 111).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using AND instead of XOR in the Boolean difference.
- Forgetting that the test must set the line to the *opposite* of the stuck value.

scenes.text: Roth invented a symbol D meaning: good circuit 1, faulty circuit 0.
The algorithm drives D through gates until it reaches an output.

steps.title: D-calculus
steps.body: Values: 0, 1, X, **D** (good=1/faulty=0), **D'** (good=0/faulty=1). Gate evaluation works pairwise on (good, faulty). Examples: AND(D,1)=D, AND(D,0)=0, AND(D,D')=0, OR(D,0)=D, NOT(D)=D', NAND(D,1)=D'.

steps.title: D-algorithm steps
steps.body:
- **D-frontier:** gates whose output is X with at least one D/D' input.
- **J-frontier:** gates whose output value is set but not yet justified by its inputs.
1. Place D/D' at the fault site (activation).
2. **Propagate:** pick a gate on the D-frontier, assign non-controlling values to its other inputs (AND: 1, OR: 0); imply forward and backward.
3. Repeat until D reaches a PO, then **justify** the J-frontier by choosing inputs, backtracking if conflicts arise.
D-algorithm may choose any internal line, so its search space is large.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: z = (a·b)+c, fault: line g=a·b s-a-0. Activation: g = D, needs a=1, b=1. Propagation through OR needs c=0 → z = D. Test: abc = 110. Good z=1, faulty z=0.

steps.title: Conflict example
steps.body: If c is also forced to 1 by another path through reconvergent fanout, c=0 and c=1 conflict: backtrack to another D-frontier choice. A fault is **redundant** if all choices are exhausted.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the controlling value on side inputs (kills D).
- Writing D for a stuck-at-1 activation: it is D'.

options: X output and a D input
quiz.why: They are candidates to propagate D.

quiz.q: If every D-frontier choice leads to conflict, the fault is:

scenes.text: Goel noticed that choosing values at internal lines wastes effort.
PODEM only assigns primary inputs, simulates, and backtracks on PI choices.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body:
1. Choose an **objective** (line, value): first activate the fault, later pick a D-frontier gate and set a side input to non-controlling.
2. **Backtrace** the objective to a PI along X-valued lines, inverting the value across inverting gates; choose easy/hard inputs using SCOAP.
3. Assign the PI, **imply** by forward 5-valued simulation.
4. If a D reaches a PO: success. If the D-frontier empties or the fault site cannot be activated: **backtrack** (flip the last PI assignment). If both values of the first PI fail: redundant.
Search space is only 2^(number of PIs), and it is complete.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
z = NAND(a, b), y = NAND(z, c) = PO. Fault: z s-a-1.
Objective z=0 → backtrace: NAND needs both inputs 1 → a=1, b=1 (z=D'). Next objective: propagate through y: c must be 1 (non-controlling). Assign c=1 → y = NAND(D',1) = D. Test **abc = 111**, good y=1... check: good z=0, y=1; faulty z=1, y=0. D at output.

steps.title: Backtrace inversion
steps.body: Objective: set the output of an AND-NOT chain n2 = NOT(n1), n1 = AND(a,b) to 1. n2=1 needs n1=0, which needs a=0 (easiest controlling) → PI assignment a=0 (two inversions in the counting: 1→0 through NOT, 0 stays 0 to input of AND).

steps.title: Why PODEM is faster
steps.body: The D-algorithm backtracks over internal lines, PODEM only over PIs, and every assignment is checked by plain simulation, so inconsistency never appears.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to invert the objective value across NAND/NOR/NOT in backtrace.
- Giving up before exhausting both values of each PI.

lessons.title: Random patterns, LFSR and test length

story.title: Let the LFSR do the work

scenes.text: A hundred thousand pseudo-random vectors cost nothing to generate on chip.
But a 12-input AND output s-a-0 is detected by only one vector in 4096.

steps.title: Detection probability
steps.body: If a fault is detected by a random vector with probability p, the probability that N vectors detect it is **1 − (1−p)^N**. For confidence C: **N = ln(1−C) / ln(1−p)** ≈ −ln(1−C)/p for small p.

steps.title: LFSR
steps.body: A linear feedback shift register with a primitive polynomial of degree n cycles through 2^n − 1 non-zero states (all-zero state is locked). Characteristic polynomial example: x^4 + x + 1 generates a maximal-length sequence of **15** states. LFSRs produce pseudo-random vectors; they are cheap in area.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: For an n-input AND, output s-a-0 needs all inputs 1: p = 2^-n. For n = 16 and C = 0.99, N ≈ 4.605 × 65536 ≈ 301,800 vectors. Such **random-pattern-resistant** faults need weighted patterns, test points or deterministic top-up patterns.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking an LFSR generates 2^n states (the all-zero state is excluded for XOR-feedback LFSRs).
- Ignoring random-pattern-resistant logic such as wide AND/OR trees and comparators.

lessons.title: Why sequential circuits are hard to test

story.title: The counter that never reaches its state

scenes.text: A 32-bit counter must reach 2^31 to flip its top bit; ATPG would need billions of clocks.
Designers add a way to load and read flip-flops directly.

steps.title: Problems
steps.body: Internal flip-flops are neither directly controllable nor observable. ATPG must use **time-frame expansion** (iterative logic array): unroll the circuit k clock cycles, treat each frame as combinational, and apply combinational ATPG. Depth grows, the fault appears in every frame (multiple fault), initialisation needs a synchronising sequence and tests are very long.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: A circuit has 3 flip-flops and needs 5 time frames. The unrolled combinational model has 5 copies of the logic: if one frame has 200 gates, the model has about 1000 gates, and the fault site is replicated in 5 places.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: A 32-bit synchronous counter: to test the MSB s-a-0 the count must reach 2^31 ≈ 2.1×10^9 clocks. At 100 MHz that is 21.5 seconds for one pattern, versus microseconds with scan load.

steps.title: DFT remedies
steps.body: Ad-hoc: reset lines, test points, breaking feedback. Structured: **scan**, **BIST**, boundary scan.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming sequential ATPG scales to full-chip industrial designs.
- Forgetting initialisation: unknown (X) flip-flop states block fault propagation.

lessons.title: Scan cells, scan chains and the scan test protocol

story.title: Turning flip-flops into a shift register

scenes.text: A multiplexer in front of each flip-flop selects functional data or the previous cell.
In test mode the flops form a long shift register: shift in a state, pulse the clock once, shift out the response.

steps.title: Mux-D scan cell
steps.body: Inputs: D (functional), SI (scan in), SE (scan enable). When SE=1 the flop loads SI, otherwise D. Chains connect Q of one cell to SI of the next. Pins: SI, SO, SE (shared with functional pins if needed).

steps.title: Protocol
steps.body:
1. **Scan-in (shift):** SE=1; apply L clocks for chain length L.
2. **Capture:** SE=0; apply 1 functional clock; primary inputs applied, primary outputs measured before capture.
3. **Scan-out:** SE=1; shift out responses while shifting in the next pattern (overlapped).
Other styles: **LSSD** (level sensitive, two non-overlapping clocks, master-slave latches L1/L2) and clocked scan.

steps.title: Test time
steps.body: P patterns, chain length L, shift clock period T: with overlap, cycles ≈ P·(L+1) + L. Example: P = 1000, L = 500: cycles = 1000×501 + 500 = **501,500** cycles; at 50 MHz scan clock = 10.03 ms. Splitting into 5 chains of 100: cycles = 1000×101 + 100 = 101,100 → 2.02 ms, a 5× reduction.

steps.title: Area overhead
steps.body: A mux-D adds one 2:1 mux to each flop. If a flop is 20 units of area and the mux is 6, overhead is 6/20 = 30% of flop area; if flops are 25% of the chip, total ≈ 7.5%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the last capture/unload in cycle counts.
- Using the functional clock frequency for shift when the scan clock can be slower to limit shift power.

lessons.title: Scan design rules, DFT-friendly RTL and partial scan

story.title: The gated clock that broke the chain

scenes.text: DRC flags a clock generated by logic; scan cells behind it cannot shift.
The fix: bypass the gate with a test-mode mux.

steps.title: Typical DFT DRC
steps.body:
- All flop clocks must be controllable from a pin in test mode (bypass internal dividers and gates).
- Asynchronous set/reset controllable in test mode.
- No combinational feedback loops; no uninitialised latches.
- Tri-state buses: only one driver enabled in test; bus keepers.
- Avoid X-sources (uninitialised RAMs): add bypass.
- Lock-up latches between clock domains in a chain to avoid hold violations.

steps.title: Partial scan and multiple domains
steps.body: **Full scan:** all flops scanned. **Partial scan:** break feedback loops first (selecting a minimum feedback vertex set), lower area, but needs sequential ATPG. Multiple clock domains use separate chains or ordered chains by domain with lock-up latches.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Chain with 4 flops: 1000 patterns. If a design has 8000 flops and a tester allows 16 scan channels, chain length = 8000/16 = 500 flops; shift cycles ≈ 1000×501 = 501,000.

steps.title: Hold fix
steps.body: Between a flop in CLK domain A and the next in B with skew 0.3 ns and clk-to-q 0.2 ns, hold may fail (0.2 < 0.3 + hold time). A lock-up latch transparent when the clock is low retimes data by half a cycle.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving an internally generated reset uncontrollable in test.
- Mixing rising- and falling-edge flops without a lock-up latch or order change.

lessons.title: IEEE 1149.1 boundary scan and the TAP controller

story.title: Testing a board with no bed of nails

scenes.text: BGA packages hide their pins under the chip, so probes cannot touch the solder joints.
Each IO has a boundary-scan cell; the chips daisy-chain on four wires.

steps.title: Pins and registers
steps.body: Mandatory pins: **TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO**; optional TRST*. Registers: Instruction Register (IR), Bypass (1 bit), Boundary-Scan Register (BSR), optional IDCODE and user registers.

steps.title: TAP controller
steps.body: A 16-state FSM driven by TMS on the rising edge of TCK. Holding **TMS = 1 for five clocks** always returns to Test-Logic-Reset. Path to scan data: Run-Test/Idle → Select-DR-Scan → Capture-DR → Shift-DR → Exit1-DR → Update-DR. Instruction scan uses Select-IR-Scan similarly. TDI is sampled and TDO changes on the **falling** edge.

steps.title: Instructions
steps.body:
- **BYPASS:** 1-bit register between TDI and TDO (all ones code).
- **SAMPLE/PRELOAD:** snapshot or preload the BSR without disturbing function.
- **EXTEST:** drive BSR values to pins to test interconnects.
- **INTEST/RUNBIST (optional), IDCODE** (32-bit device ID, LSB = 1).

steps.title: Worked example: chain length
steps.body: Three chips with BSR 200, 150 and 80 bits and 4-bit IRs. Loading instructions: 12 shifts. EXTEST data scan: 430 shifts. With the middle chip in BYPASS: 200 + 1 + 80 = **281**.

steps.title: Interconnect test
steps.body: Number of walking-1 vectors for N nets is N; a counting sequence needs only ceil(log2(N+2)) vectors: for 62 nets, log2(64)=6 vectors.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying TDO changes on the rising edge.
- Forgetting the IR must be loaded before every different DR operation.

story.title: Too much data for the tester

scenes.text: A 100-million-gate SoC needs terabits of scan data.
A decompressor expands a few tester channels into hundreds of internal chains.

steps.title: Why it works
steps.body: Test cubes have only ~1–5% **care bits**; the rest are free. A decompressor (linear, e.g. LFSR with phase shifter or XOR network) maps compressed seeds to full patterns. A compactor (XOR tree/MISR) compresses output; X values must be masked or tolerated.

steps.title: Metrics
steps.body: **Compression ratio** = (uncompressed data volume) / (compressed data volume); test time ratio is similar. Typical 10× to 100×+. Encoding a cube with s care bits needs about s + 20 seed bits.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Uncompressed: 2,000 patterns × 400,000 flops = 800 Mbit. With 8 channels feeding 800 internal chains: chain length = 400,000/800 = 500; cycles ≈ 2,000×501 = 1.0 M instead of (8 chains of 50,000) 2,000×50,001 = 100 M → **100× less test time**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring that more internal chains increase shift power and routing.
- Letting unmasked X reach a XOR compactor: it masks all other bits in that cycle.

lessons.title: Delay testing: transition faults, LOC, LOS, path delay

scenes.text: A resistive via adds 150 ps to a path. At a slow tester clock the chip passes; at 2 GHz it fails.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Transition fault test
steps.body:
Two vectors: V1 initialises the node, V2 launches the transition and propagates it to a capture flop; capture happens at the **functional clock speed**. With scan, V1 is shifted in and V2 is obtained in one of two ways:
- **Launch-on-capture (LOC, broadside):** V2 is the functional response to V1 — two fast capture pulses, SE stays low; simpler timing, lower coverage (V2 restricted).
- **Launch-on-shift (LOS, skewed-load):** V2 is the shifted-by-one version of V1; last shift is launch, then SE must switch fast to capture — requires a fast SE signal; higher coverage.

steps.title: Path delay
steps.body: Tests a specific path for the cumulative delay; **robust** tests are hazard-free; **non-robust** may be invalidated. Number of paths grows exponentially, so only critical paths (from STA) are tested.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Functional clock 500 MHz (2 ns). Path delay design target 1.7 ns; a defect adds 0.5 ns → 2.2 ns > 2 ns − setup (0.1 ns) → fails only at speed. A test clock of 50 MHz (20 ns) would pass it: coverage requires at-speed.

steps.title: Fault count
steps.body: Transition faults = 2 per node (slow-to-rise, slow-to-fall), same count as stuck-at, but each test is two-vector.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using LOS without a fast scan-enable.
- Treating false paths as testable: they must be constrained out.

lessons.title: IDDQ testing, diagnosis and yield learning

scenes.text: A shorted node makes a static CMOS circuit draw microamps instead of nanoamps.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: IDDQ
steps.body: In static CMOS the quiescent supply current is normally tiny (leakage only). Bridges, gate-oxide shorts and stuck-on transistors raise it. Apply a vector, wait for settling, measure IDD. A threshold (e.g. 10× the normal) flags a defect. In deep submicron nodes leakage is large and varies, so use **delta IDDQ** or current ratios.

steps.title: Diagnosis
steps.body: Fail logs from scan identify failing flops and patterns; **effect-cause** and **cause-effect** analysis with fault dictionaries locate defect sites for physical failure analysis, driving yield learning (systematic defects vs random).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A die has leakage 40 µA nominal with 5% spread across patterns. A bridge adds 120 µA. Measured 160 µA ≫ 40×1.05 = 42 µA → flagged. In a 2 mA leakage design the same 120 µA is only 6% above nominal and is lost in noise.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying a fixed IDDQ limit across process corners.
- Measuring before the circuit has settled.

statements.s: IDDQ is effective regardless of process leakage.
statements.why: High background leakage hides defect currents.
They create a static current path between VDD and GND.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- Williams-Brown: **DL = 1 − Y^(1−T)**.
- Faults: 2N uncollapsed; n-input basic gate collapses to n+2; checkpoints = PIs + fanout branches.
- Coverage: FC = D/T; test coverage = D/(T−U); effectiveness = (D+U)/T.
- SCOAP: AND CC1 = ΣCC1+1, CC0 = minCC0+1; OR dual; NOT swaps +1; PO CO = 0.
- Boolean difference ∂f/∂x = f(x=0)⊕f(x=1).
- Random test length: N = ln(1−C)/ln(1−p).
- LFSR period 2^n−1; MISR alias 2^-n.
- Scan test cycles ≈ P(L+1)+L; L = F/chains.
- March C- = 10n; MATS+ = 5n; March B = 17n.
- JTAG: TLR after 5 × TMS=1; BYPASS 1 bit.

lessons.title: Lab: Fault simulation and coverage of a small circuit

scenes.text: The lab manual asks you to find the coverage of a 4-vector test set on a 2-gate circuit.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Aim and circuit
steps.body: Aim: perform single stuck-at fault simulation for z = (a·b) + c. Lines: a, b, c, g (=a·b), z → 5 lines = 10 faults. Apparatus: Verilog simulator or fault simulator.

steps.title: Procedure and observation
steps.body:
Vectors abc: 110, 001, 101, 011.
- 110: good z=1: detects a/0, b/0, g/0, z/0 (c=0 so g propagates). 
- 001: good z=1: detects c/0, z/0.
- 101: good z = 1; detects c/0? c=1 forces z=1 either way: detects z/0 only... 
- 011: z=1, detects c/0, z/0.
Detected so far: a/0, b/0, g/0, c/0, z/0 = 5. The s-a-1 faults need vectors producing good 0 (e.g. 000, 010, 100): none of the four vectors has good z=0 so **no s-a-1 fault is detected**. Coverage = 5/10 = **50%**. Adding 000 (detects c/1, z/1), 010 (detects b/1... g/1), 100 detects a/1 gives 100%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that s-a-1 faults need good value 0.
- Dropping the test table units.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – Plan the test strategy for a small SoC

scenes.text: A 50 M-gate SoC has 2 million flops, 40 SRAMs and a 1.2 mm² analog block. You propose the test architecture.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Brief
steps.body: Choose DFT for logic, memories, IO and at-speed test, and compute the scan time.

steps.title: Worked solution
steps.body:
- Logic: full scan with compression 50×; 2,000,000 flops, 1000 internal chains → L = 2000; 6,000 patterns (compressed ATPG) → cycles = 6000×2001 ≈ 12.0 M; at 100 MHz = 120 ms.
- Memories: MBIST per SRAM group running March C- in parallel; the largest 2 Mbit (256K×8) memory: 10×262,144 = 2.62 M ops at 200 MHz = 13.1 ms.
- IO: boundary scan for board test, IDCODE.
- At-speed: LOC transition patterns with on-chip PLL pulse generator.
- Analog: loopback or BIST via ADC/DAC; not ATPG.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Justify each choice and state the expected coverage (stuck-at ≥ 98%, transition ≥ 90%).
